From Dame Millicent Fawcett—
I heartily welcome THE ELECTRICAL AGE FOR WOMEN, and wish it every success. * * * * *
From Sir Hugo Hirst, Bart.—
Indications are plenty showing that electricity is bound to change our industrial, social and home lives. Nothing seems more natural than that women should play an important part in this gradual transformation.

title: Major-General; Sir
brief_context: Comments on electrical production and the technical press.
article_title: Greetings from other public Men and Women
brief_extract:
My best wishes for a long and prosperous career. * * * * *
From Major-General Sir Philip Nash—
I have always thought that Great Britain possesses not only first-class electrical brains, and facilities equal to them for the production of electrical material, but it also possesses a first-class electrical technical press. It wants, however, more and more articles in the public press to educate the people of this country to the great advantages which a greater use of electricity can bring in the domestic lives of the people.

title: Lady
brief_context: Delivering a speech on women's service and electrical energy.
brief_extract: The main principles of the Bill must be preserved, but any alteration which may be proved to be good we are quite willing to consider, and should welcome the whole-hearted co-operation of anybody or any body of institutes who are concerned in this great and important measure—(cheers). Lady Cowan (Vice-President, E.A.W.).—Service with women has grown up with women, and as woman's services for the men and for the world are as old as the Garden of Eden, the whole idea of service in a woman's life has become embodied even in the legends and sagas of our own race. So that we women are well accustomed to the idea of service in that way, but it is left to these later days to find that the great forces of Nature are being commandeered for the first time in the service of women, and that we are for the first time in the history of civilisation in control of a tremendous power and energy which, if properly directed and utilised, will not only ease the burden of women's lives but of the weary lives of the vast majority of workers, not only in this country but throughout the whole world.

title: Colonel
brief_context: Mentioned by Lady Cowan as a previous speaker.
brief_extract: So that we women are well accustomed to the idea of service in that way, but it is left to these later days to find that the great forces of Nature are being commandeered for the first time in the service of women, and that we are for the first time in the history of civilisation in control of a tremendous power and energy which, if properly directed and utilised, will not only ease the burden of women's lives but of the weary lives of the vast majority of workers, not only in this country but throughout the whole world. England has always been a leader, and often the leader, in the great unfolding and in the great amelioration and progress of the human race, but, as Colonel Ashley has just told us, we have somehow lagged behind, particularly in the development of electrical appliances and mechanical devices, and have been outstripped in the race in this particular development by other countries, and even by the daughter States of our own Empire. I think that this Association is going to do an immense deal to make up that leeway, and is going to give that necessary encouragement to patriotic-minded manufacturers by creating a demand for these mechanical and electrical devices, for the want of which we are suffering so much in our homes to-day.

title: Colonel
role: Minister in charge of the Bill
brief_context: Proposed the toast the speaker is responding to.
brief_extract: That is one of the reasons why the workers in America and Canada are so much happier, more prosperous and contented than here, because they have less drudgery and more time and leisure for outdoor life and for those amusements and pleasures which are their legitimate right. It is because I firmly believe that this association of women for the propaganda work in electrical appliances and labour-saving devices is going to be a success, is going to lighten and ease the burdens of the women in this country, that I have great pleasure in responding to the toast proposed by Colonel Ashley, to whom we owe a deep debt of gratitude as Minister in charge of the Bill which is going through the Committee stage of the House of Commons to-day, and to whom we look to be the herald of that millennium of feminine emancipation from drudgery, to which we look forward with such unspeakable relief—(applause). Sir Hugo Hirst, Bart., proposing the toast, The Electrical Association for Women.

brief_extract: My dress is all crushed and 'tis Saturday afternoon. The iron won't work and there is no possibility of getting it mended till Monday, and everyone is cross and the world is horrid"; and if Eva had lived in the last century she would undoubtedly have wept, but being a 1926 miss, she merely set her lips very tight and proceeded to "tidy up" with disconcerting vehemence. 'Tis always the little things that count, and when Eva's troubles are analyzed they will probably be found to have all their origin in some trivial displacement of a bit of metal—as easily remedied as sewing on a button—if only we knew where to find the ill.

brief_context: The owner of the iron being repaired for a party.
brief_extract: In nine cases out of ten, when an iron won't work, you will find that the copper of the flex has broken off a little way from this attachment. If this is the case with Eva's iron, we will just cut off the broken bit, clean back the flex a little way, and screw it up again in the attachment exactly as before. As we have just taken this all to pieces, it is quite simple to reverse the operation and to put it all together again in exactly the same way as it came to bits.

brief_extract:
By Len Chaloner
Though we may be quite ready to thank electricity for lighting, heating, labour-saving devices, and many of the amenities of civilisation generally, it is still something of a surprise to learn that electricity played a part in the discovery of artificial silk. Many scientists had foreseen that artificially produced silk would, some day, become a possibility, but though Chardonnet, a Frenchman, was the first to take out a patent for an artificial silk in 1884, the early efforts of Sir William Crookes and Mr. Swan in 1882-1884, in experiments to produce a structureless thread for lamp filaments, led them to the observation that a thread for textile purposes, with the appearance and characteristics of silk, could also be made.

brief_extract:
134 The Electrical Age

Wedding Presents! By Len Chaloner

In what must assuredly have been the "good old times" from the bridegroom's point of view, there was no question of what to do with the "white elephant" wedding present, for there were none! We have it, on the contrary, on the best authority, that about eight hundred and fifty years ago, a little before the Norman conquest, loans were raised for the newly married ones to start them in their "Paradise enow." What better precedent could be found for the making of practical wedding offerings, and what more practical form could they take than electrical equipment for the home?

Nursery Magic!! By Len Chaloner

A visit to a modern nursery is prone to make us feel a little like the traditional Rip Van Winkle, so amazing are the changes that have taken place in the last few years. article_title: The Work of The Electricity Commissioners.
brief_extract: Thus the time was ripe for bringing about a comprehensive system of Generation, Transmission and Distribution; during 1918 the Board of Trade set up important committees, upon whose recommendation the next step was taken to ensure an adequate and economical supply of electrical energy for all classes of consumers, special regard being paid to the need of those Industries dependent upon a cheap supply of power for their development. By the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1919, the general supervision of the supply of electricity in the country was placed in the hands of five Commissioners, and the Chairman appointed by the then Minister of Transport was Sir John Snell. The Commissioners were men of great electrical or financial knowledge and experience, and the Chairman brought with him also much goodwill, which proved of great value in the many delicate tasks confronting him and his colleagues.

Sir Andrew Duncan said that in coming to the luncheon he had a private and unofficial undertaking that he was to be allowed to remain a silent observer of the proceedings, and he believed Lady Snell took the view that this understanding would not be breached, for she ascribed to the popular belief that Scotsmen had such vast experience in receiving hospitality that they were able at any moment to return thanks for it. All he would say was that he advised them not to build their hopes quite so high as Sir Philip Nash had recommended them to do. title: Sir
brief_context: Discovered the light spectrum, proving invisible radiant energy.
brief_extract:
During the Dark Ages, the practice of heliotherapy fell entirely into oblivion, and there was no appreciable revival until the latter end of the 18th Century. There is no space in this article to deal with the progress of knowledge of the value of Sunlight treatment, but the discovery of the spectrum by Sir Isaac Newton and the experiments of Ritter, Herschell and others proved the existence of invisible radiant energy, and thus opened up the field to a fuller knowledge of the beneficial Ultra Violet Ray of the natural Sunlight. It is interesting to note the following from Sir Oliver Lodge:—

"When the most efficient parts of Sunlight are excluded the organisms which flourish are of the lowest kind ; and the higher organisms are apt to succumb to their ravages when unaided by the beneficial influence of Sunlight."
The value of sunlight is now universally acknowledged, and we are all fully aware of the stimulation in health and vitality which sunlight gives.

brief_extract: Partridge, B.Sc. So many enquiries have reached us recently as to how a supply of Electricity can be obtained in Rural Districts, especially from Women's Institutes, that we have asked Miss Partridge, who has had considerable experience in such matters, to write an article setting forth the position. What a lot of ink has been spilt, what volumes of hot air have been expended on the subject of electricity for country districts.

title: Mr.
brief_context: Mentioned as leader of the government that passed the 1926 Act.
Person advised to contact regarding electricity lighting rights.
brief_extract: Then enquire from the Town Clerk or Clerk to the Local Council, if anyone owns the lighting rights over your district. If no one owns it, or has staked out any claim to it, write to the Director of the E.A.W. There is, however, very little uncovered country now, and you will, quite probably, find yourself in the area of a Power Company or a Supply Company.

brief_context: Mentioned by the author regarding future writing opportunities.
brief_extract: The usual limit of time given to a Supply Company to lay down mains is two years, but it is longer in sparsely populated districts. I hope the Editor will ask me to write on the same subject in twelve months' time. Then I may have a very different tale to tell, but at present history is being made so fast in the matter of rural electricity supply that what I write to-day may well be quite out of date by the time it appears in print.

title: Miss
brief_context: Presided over the first Annual General Meeting.
brief_extract: The first Annual General Meeting was held in the Lecture Theatre, Carliol House, on April 25th. Miss Balls was in the chair, and a representative audience of members, delegates from the Women's Institutes and Women's Co-operation Guilds numbering 80, gathered together. Miss Balls, in introducing Miss Haslett, said that she thought the annual report was very satisfactory and that the North East Coast Branch had done a great deal in educating themselves, and now we were required to do something to bring the use of electricity to the help of the intelligent women workers, as it was not only a question for the rich, but was a necessity to everyone.

brief_extract: . Gladys Sharp. Lovers of the English countryside are sad people in these enlightened days for, as time goes on, it becomes apparent that seemingly civilisation and beauty cannot go hand in hand.

brief_context: The namesake of the workshop for disabled ex-service men.
brief_extract: Leaving the Ashtead potters busily making things to delight our eyes and brighten our homes we will take a short journey to another, smaller workshop in Surrey where electricity is doing its good turn every day. The Frederick Milner workshop for disabled ex-service men is a large airy room in which about a dozen men, all of them declared totally unfit for any occupation, work under the very best conditions making electrically-heated blankets and stocking driers. When our unhappy climate fails to pour health-giving sunshine through the many windows it is only necessary to switch on and from the lofty ceiling artificial sunlight is diffused from evenly-spaced lamps which also light the room and, of course, help to warm it.

Mentioned as the only man with good intentions for Parliament.
brief_extract: From the inception of the public supply of Electricity, up till the time of the Great War, and, indeed, later even than that, it was the opinion of a great many people engaged in the industry that one of the factors seriously hampering its expansion was the legislation which Parliament, in its wisdom, had imposed on it. I have heard it said that only one man ever entered Parliament with good intentions, and his name was Guy Fawkes. It is now generally agreed that legislation is more often than not behind the times.

brief_context: The Williamson Committee of 1918 is named after him.
brief_extract: It is from this latter point of view that my audience this afternoon will principally consider the working and the effects of this Act. After the War, a Committee was set up, called "The Electric Power Supply Committee" (generally known as the Williamson Committee of 1918). This Committee recommended the division of the country into areas, the appointment of Joint Boards of Control, of Generating Stations to be purchased, the best of these stations to be kept running and the supply organised on a regional basis.

title: Lord
brief_context: Presided over the committee investigating the national electrical supply problem.
brief_extract:
In January, 1925, the Right Hon. Wilfrid Ashley, the Minister of Transport, appointed another Committee, presided over by Lord Weir, and consisting of Lord Forres and Sir Hardman Lever. This Committee had the assistance of the Electricity Commissioners and other eminent engineers in dealing with their subject; their terms of reference being "To review the national problem of the supply of Electrical Energy and to present a report on the broad lines of policy which should be adopted to ensure its most efficient and effective development."

The report, which was handled with the greatest secrecy, became substantially the subject matter of the Electricity (Supply) Act of 1926, an Act which has had showered on it a great deal of criticism, and from which the benefits are still to come.

IN LIGHTER VEIN. The Letters of Lulu. My Dear Flip,

brief_context: The recipient of the letter from Lulu.
brief_extract:
The Letters of Lulu. My Dear Flip,
Of course you've heard the news?—your own Lulu one of the world's workers, learning to be an electrical engineeress—on one of those grid things you read about in the newspapers. My Dear, it's stupendous; of course I don't wear those filthy pull-over things and go about with a tureen of oil.

brief_context: Mentioned as the source of Lulu's new dress.
brief_extract:
(Juice, my Dear, is scientific for electricity, aren't I just too highbrow for anything?)
Of course, I didn't learn all about everything at once, made just the teeniest mistakes at first. Only the second day I was there I was left all alone, when in walked the most gorgeous man, my Dear, so I said now I'll show them all what I can do (I had my new dress on—from Isobelle's) so I shot forward and dazzled him with the most devastating smile and he simply reeled, my Dear, I just stunned him. I said do let me show you our very latest fire, it's just sweet, and priceless for lighting cigarettes (the boys had shown this to me) think what a ghastly number of matches you save.

brief_context: The head of the showroom where Lulu works.
brief_extract: Of course, he would ask me how much current the fiery thing consumed, but as he didn't say juice, I knew in a minute he hadn't the foggiest idea, so I just said you could burn it for hours and hours and it only used the weeniest current. My Dear, I felt I had raised a howling impression, for his face just skidded when someone came in, he melted away, and later they told me he was the Chief, a sort of headman, in other words the boss. I could have screamed!

brief_context: A visitor to the showroom described by Lulu as 'that cat'.
brief_extract: I could have screamed! Of course, I felt rather reduced but all the men were too crushingly kind and I soon recovered when one of them brought me a stunning box of chocolates and I was just submerged in them, when in comes the Chief and with him that cat Popsie Wimble so I just slid the chocolates like lightning under the top of an oven and just plopped the lid to. My Dear, she went round all the gadgets and stopped bang in front the very oven and the Chief turned on a switch and horrors the infernal old sizzler began to stew my chocolates and there was that fiend Popsie Wimble asking the most iniquitous questions and she doesn't know how many amps go to the volt.

article_title: The Newcastle Conference: OUR OVERSEA GUESTS
brief_extract: This is the first occasion on which women from different countries have been gathered together on one platform and we hope that the result of the Conference will be an International expression of the woman's point of view on matters electrical. From America we have three guests, Miss Sophia Malicki, who is Chairman of the Women's Committee of the Public Relations Section of the National Electric Light Association, is one of the most popular and well known women in the Electrical Industry in the United States. Author of the article regarding the history of sewing machines.
brief_extract:
. "Haselwurr."

Since our early childhood we have all been familiar with the sight of the Sewing Machine in the Home. In this article a fascinating picture is given of the history of the Sewing Machine, and how Electricity has stepped in to save labour and increase efficiency.

brief_context: Mentioned as the inventor of the sewing machine.
brief_extract: The pioneers of the Sewing Machine invention had little encouragement during their struggles and toil in obscurity, and often in great poverty they pursued their tasks, meeting and overcoming many obstacles; suffering also acute disappointments, but continuing undaunted because they had faith in their idea. The growth of the Sewing Machine industry can perhaps be better realised when I tell you that whereas in 1853, or about two years after the first Singer Machine was patented, the total world sales of all makes of Sewing Machines were 2,500; at the present time well over 2,000,000 Singer Sewing Machines alone are being sold every year. It can, therefore, be justly claimed that the Singer invention has probably done more to reduce the drudgery of manual labour, and at the same time has rendered service and benefit to womankind, greater than any other single invention.

article_title: Hints on Electric Lamps. ANTI-GLARE LAMPS AND THEIR COST TO USE.
brief_extract: Of all methods of illumination, it is universally agreed that where Electricity is obtainable, Electric Light far excels all others. Since the invention of the first practical electric lamp by Sir Joseph Swan, fifty years ago, we have had the carbon lamp, the metal filament vacuum lamp, and the gas-filled lamp, each one more efficient than the last both in regard to light and durability. This bright light source, however, unless entirely screened from view, causes great discomfort and even injury to the eyes, and we complain of the "glare." To eliminate this glare various types of obscured lamps have been devised, and a great stride forward has been made by the new "Pearl" and "Opal" lamps.

brief_extract: Describing a London Hospital staffed and run by women, where electricity plays an important part in remedial and curative work. The first woman to take a degree and practise as a doctor of medicine was Elizabeth Garrett Anderson, and to-day, in Euston Road, there stands the finest memorial to this pioneer that she could have wished. The Hospital which bears her name is run entirely by women for the treatment of women and children, and in the tiled entrance hall, from which all sound of the busy road outside is excluded as by a miracle, one sees oil paintings of many of the clever women who have been associated with the hospital.
